title: Nerve supply to the teeth & mouth
blurb: The trigeminal nerve and its branches, which teeth and tissues each one supplies, and how that decides the local anaesthetic.
question: The dentist is about to extract a lower left first molar and asks you to prepare for an inferior dental block plus a long buccal injection. The patient asks why they need two injections when the upper filling they had last year only needed one 'in the gum'. How would you explain it?

teach.h: The trigeminal nerve: feeling for the whole face
teach.body: There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves. The fifth, the trigeminal nerve (V), is the big one for dentistry. It carries sensation from the face, teeth, gums, palate and tongue, and it drives the muscles of mastication. It splits into three divisions: ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2) and mandibular (V3). Local anaesthetic works by blocking these nerves from carrying messages, so knowing which branch supplies which tooth tells the dentist where to inject.

children.label: Ophthalmic (V1)
children.sub: Forehead, eye, nose. Sensory. Not dental

children.label: Maxillary (V2)
children.sub: Upper teeth, palate, upper lip. Sensory only

children.label: Mandibular (V3)
children.sub: Lower teeth, tongue, lower lip. Sensory AND motor

teach.caption: V3 is the only division with motor fibres: it supplies the muscles of mastication.

teach.h: Maxillary division (V2): upper teeth and palate

children.label: Superior alveolar nerves
children.sub: Anterior: incisors and canine. Middle: premolars. Posterior: molars

children.label: Palatine nerves
children.sub: Greater palatine: back of palate. Nasopalatine: behind incisors

children.label: Infraorbital
children.sub: Upper lip, cheek, side of nose

teach.caption: The upper first molar's mesiobuccal root is often supplied by the middle superior alveolar nerve.

teach.h: Mandibular division (V3): lower teeth and tongue

children.label: Inferior alveolar
children.sub: All lower teeth on that side; mental branch to lip and chin

children.label: Lingual
children.sub: Front two-thirds of tongue, floor of mouth, lingual gum

children.label: Long buccal
children.sub: Buccal gum by the lower molars, cheek lining

teach.caption: V3 also gives motor branches to masseter, temporalis and both pterygoids.

teach.h: Why upper teeth need an infiltration and lower molars need a block
teach.body: The bone over the upper teeth is thin and porous, so anaesthetic placed in the gum beside a root tip soaks through to the nerve: an infiltration. The adult mandible has thick, dense outer bone, so infiltration rarely works for lower molars. Instead the inferior alveolar nerve is blocked where it enters the mandibular foramen on the inner ramus: an inferior dental block (IDB). The lingual nerve lies close by, so it is usually numbed at the same time.

head: Injection
Nerve
Numbs
rows: That upper tooth and buccal gum
Lower teeth on one side, lip, half the tongue
Lower front teeth and premolars, lip
teach.caption: Extractions need the gum on BOTH sides of the tooth numb, which is why a palatal or long buccal injection is often added.

teach.h: A left IDB: what goes numb
teach.caption: All lower left teeth to the midline, plus the left lower lip and chin (mental nerve) and the left side of the tongue (lingual nerve). The buccal gum by 36–38 needs the long buccal nerve.

teach.body: The facial nerve (VII) is mainly a motor nerve: it moves the muscles of facial expression. It also carries taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue (via a branch that travels with the lingual nerve) and stimulates the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands. It runs through the parotid gland. If an IDB is given too far back, anaesthetic can reach it there, causing a temporary facial palsy: the eye on that side may not close, so cover and protect it until the effect wears off.

teach.text: The INFERIOR ALVEOLAR nerve supplies the lower TEETH; the LINGUAL nerve supplies the TONGUE and lingual gum; the LONG BUCCAL supplies the buccal gum by the lower molars. And the maxillary division (V2) is sensory only: no muscles.

items: Trigeminal (V): V1 ophthalmic, V2 maxillary (upper teeth, palate), V3 mandibular (lower teeth, tongue, chewing muscles).
Upper teeth: anterior, middle and posterior superior alveolar nerves; palate: greater palatine and nasopalatine.
Lower teeth: inferior alveolar nerve, with the mental branch to the lip; tongue: lingual; buccal gum by molars: long buccal.
Upper teeth: infiltration. Lower molars in adults: IDB, plus long buccal for extractions.
Warn patients not to bite their numb lip or tongue, or test hot drinks, until feeling returns.

summary: You can now name the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve, say which branch supplies each group of teeth and the surrounding gum, palate, lip and tongue, explain why upper teeth are infiltrated while adult lower molars need an IDB and long buccal, and describe what the facial nerve does and why it matters after an IDB.

A.q: A patient's lower lip and the left side of their tongue are numb after an injection. Which injection have they most likely had?
options: A left buccal infiltration of an upper tooth
A.why: An IDB numbs the inferior alveolar nerve (teeth and, via the mental branch, the lip) and usually the nearby lingual nerve (tongue).

whyNot.0: An upper infiltration numbs an upper tooth and gum, not the lower lip or tongue.
whyNot.2: A greater palatine injection numbs the back of the palate.
whyNot.3: A long buccal injection numbs only the buccal gum and cheek lining by the lower molars.

A.q: Which nerve supplies the upper molars?
A.why: The posterior superior alveolar nerve, a branch of V2, supplies the upper molars.

whyNot.0: The anterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the upper incisors and canine.
whyNot.1: The nasopalatine nerve supplies the palatal gum behind the upper front teeth.
whyNot.3: The inferior alveolar nerve supplies the lower teeth.

A.q: Why is an infiltration usually enough for an upper tooth?
options: Upper teeth have no nerve supply
The maxillary bone is thin and porous
Upper nerves sit on the bone surface
A.why: Anaesthetic placed beside the root tip diffuses easily through the thin, porous maxillary bone to the nerve.

whyNot.0: Upper teeth are supplied by the superior alveolar nerves.
whyNot.2: The nerves run inside the bone to each root; the porous bone is what lets the solution reach them.
whyNot.3: The palate does not block pain; palatal tissues have their own nerves.

B.q: The dentist is extracting 46 and has given an IDB. Which extra injection is needed to numb the buccal gum next to it?
B.why: The buccal gum by the lower molars is supplied by the long buccal nerve, which an IDB does not reliably reach.

whyNot.0: The lingual nerve, which supplies the lingual gum, is usually numbed by the IDB already.
whyNot.1: The mental nerve supplies the lip and chin and the gum by the front teeth.
whyNot.3: The nasopalatine nerve supplies the palate behind the upper incisors.

B.q: Which division of the trigeminal nerve carries motor fibres to the muscles of mastication?
B.why: Only the mandibular division (V3) has motor fibres; it supplies the four muscles of mastication.

whyNot.0: The ophthalmic division is sensory only and serves the forehead and eye.
whyNot.1: The maxillary division is sensory only.
whyNot.2: The facial nerve is a separate cranial nerve (VII), not a trigeminal division.

B.q: Which nerve gives general sensation to the front two-thirds of the tongue?
B.why: The lingual nerve, a branch of V3, carries touch and pain from the front two-thirds of the tongue.

whyNot.1: The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue but carries no sensation.
whyNot.2: The long buccal nerve supplies the cheek lining and buccal gum.
whyNot.3: The glossopharyngeal nerve serves the back third of the tongue.

C.q: An upper central incisor needs extracting. Which nerve supplies the palatal gum behind it?
C.why: The nasopalatine nerve emerges through the incisive foramen to supply the palatal gum behind the upper front teeth.

whyNot.0: The greater palatine nerve supplies the palate further back, by the premolars and molars.
whyNot.2: The posterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the upper molars.
whyNot.3: The infraorbital nerve supplies the skin of the upper lip and cheek.

C.q: Just after an IDB, the patient cannot close the eye on that side. What should the dental nurse do?
options: Tell them it is permanent nerve damage
Give them a second IDB on the other side
Ask them to keep blinking hard
Protect the eye and tell the dentist
C.why: Anaesthetic has reached the facial nerve; the palsy is temporary, but the eye must be protected until blinking returns.

whyNot.0: This effect wears off as the anaesthetic does; it is not permanent damage.
whyNot.1: Another injection would not help and is not the nurse's decision.
whyNot.2: They cannot close the eye properly, so it needs protecting, not exercising.

C.q: Which statement about the inferior alveolar nerve is correct?
options: It runs in the mandibular canal
It is a branch of the facial nerve
C.why: It enters the mandibular foramen and runs through the mandibular canal beneath the lower teeth.

whyNot.0: Its mental branch leaves through the mental foramen; the nerve enters at the mandibular foramen.
whyNot.1: The palatal gum is supplied by branches of the maxillary division.
whyNot.3: It is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

reteach.title: Think of it as the wiring in a house
reteach.question: Imagine the trigeminal nerve as the main cable into a house, splitting into three circuits. Which circuit do you switch off for each job?

blocks.body: Circuit 1 (V1) lights the top floor: forehead and eyes. You never switch it off for dentistry. Circuit 2 (V2) runs the upper jaw: each upper tooth has its own nearby wire in thin, crumbly bone, so you can switch it off locally with an infiltration. Circuit 3 (V3) runs the lower jaw. Its main wire, the inferior alveolar nerve, is buried in thick bone, so you switch it off at the fuse box, where it enters the mandibular foramen: that is the IDB. Side wires (lingual, long buccal) may need their own switch.

rows.label: Where
values: Inner ramus, near the mandibular foramen

rows.label: Why it works
values: Blocks the nerve before it enters bone

rows.label: Numbs
values: All teeth on that side, lip, half tongue

blocks.text: A numb LIP after an IDB is a sign it has WORKED (mental branch of the inferior alveolar nerve). A drooping FACE is not expected: that is the facial nerve.

explain.body: V1 ophthalmic (eye and forehead, not dental), V2 maxillary (upper teeth, palate, upper lip; sensory only), V3 mandibular (lower teeth, tongue, lower lip; sensory and motor to the chewing muscles).

items.label: mandibular: lower teeth, tongue, chewing muscles

test.q: Which division of the trigeminal nerve supplies the upper teeth?
test.why: The maxillary division (V2) supplies the upper teeth through the superior alveolar nerves.

whyNot.0: The ophthalmic division supplies the eye and forehead.
whyNot.1: The mandibular division supplies the lower teeth.
whyNot.2: The long buccal nerve is a branch of V3, not a division.

explain.body: Anterior superior alveolar: incisors and canine. Middle superior alveolar: premolars. Posterior superior alveolar: molars. The palate: greater palatine at the back, nasopalatine behind the incisors.

explain.caption: Upper right molars: posterior superior alveolar nerve (buccally) and greater palatine nerve (palatally).

test.q: Which nerve supplies the upper premolars?
test.why: The middle superior alveolar nerve supplies the upper premolars (and often the mesiobuccal root of the first molar).

whyNot.1: The anterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the incisors and canine.
whyNot.2: The inferior alveolar nerve supplies the lower teeth.
whyNot.3: The nasopalatine nerve supplies the palatal gum behind the incisors.

explain.body: The inferior alveolar nerve supplies all the lower teeth on its side; its mental branch exits to the lip and chin. The lingual nerve supplies the front two-thirds of the tongue, floor of mouth and lingual gum. The long buccal nerve supplies the buccal gum by the molars.

test.q: A patient has a numb tongue for weeks after a lower wisdom tooth removal. Which nerve is most likely affected?
test.why: The lingual nerve lies close to the lower third molars and carries sensation from the front two-thirds of the tongue.

whyNot.0: Inferior alveolar nerve damage causes a numb lip and chin, not tongue.
whyNot.2: The long buccal nerve supplies the cheek lining and buccal gum.
whyNot.3: The mental nerve supplies the lower lip and chin.

explain.body: Cranial nerve VII. It moves the muscles of facial expression, carries taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue and drives the submandibular and sublingual glands. It passes through the parotid gland, where a misplaced IDB can reach it.

test.q: Which of these is a job of the facial nerve?
options: Moving the lip and cheek muscles
test.why: The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression, including orbicularis oris and buccinator.

whyNot.0: The inferior alveolar nerve (V3) supplies the lower teeth.
whyNot.1: Masseter is supplied by V3 of the trigeminal.
whyNot.3: The palate is supplied by the palatine branches of V2.
